pr_title: Update RSA keygen to use sp800-56b by default and fix infinite loop.
pr_body:
Fixes #11742
Fixes #11764

The newer RSA sp800-56b algorithm is being used for the normal case of a non multiprime key of at least length 2048.
Insecure key lengths and multiprime RSA will use the old method.

Bad public exponents are no longer allowed (i.e values less than 65537 or even). Values such as 2 that would cause a infinite loop now result in an error. The value of 3 has been marked as deprecated but is still allowed for legacy purposes.

So could you please add this test (and maybe, test for 512 bits until it is forbidden totally)?

> @slontis does pkeygen works for you?

yes..
I confirm that #11764 works now (without applying this changes)

> So could you please add this test (and maybe, test for 512 bits until it is forbidden totally)?

With the changes in this PR it now chooses 512 as the keysize in 15-test_genrsa.t.
Added a test case specifically for 2048 bits also so that it covers the normal case also.

It's my understanding that the method we implement (B.3.6 Generation of Probable Primes with Conditions Based on Auxiliary Probable Primes) is required for smaller keys, but that for keys starting at 2048 bit we can use B.3.3 Generation of Random Primes that are Probably Prime. And we're only allowed to generate 2048 or larger keys in FIPS mode.

B.3.3 is very close to what we do now, with 2 exceptions:
- We round sqrt(2) to 2 bits, which the B.3.6 implementation also did initially.
- If it's not a prime, instead of generating a new random number, we add 2. It's at least my understanding that this does not generate a bias, but it's clearly not what FIPS 186-4 has.

So it surprises me that we're going to do just the opposite, use B.3.3 for short keys, while we should use B.3.6 for short keys. So I suggest that we always use B.3.6, except for multi prime.

PS: The B.3.6 algorithm actually does the search by adding 2, it's just slower then our probable_prime() that does the same, except probably_prime() optimizes the trial division.

If we're only going to use the old for multi prime, we can
consider changing the prime generation to only set 1 top bit, and
then check that the multiprime actually has enough enough bits.

The logic was very simple for the change. i.e:

Use the newer keygen code for fips and the normal case where possible.
For other existing cases such as multiprime (and weak keys that should not really be used) use the old method.

Please submit a PR if you wish to change the old code.

issue_context.title: RSA keygen regression
issue_context.body:
beldmit@manul$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=`pwd` apps/openssl genpkey  -algorithm rsa -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:512 -out key.pem
Error generating key

beldmit@manul$ git bisect bad
5e77b79a8c47f0801f656cfccfcbaaa3ca1035b4 is the first bad commit
commit 5e77b79a8c47f0801f656cfccfcbaaa3ca1035b4
Author: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
Date:   Thu May 7 15:31:05 2020 +1000

    Remove gen_get_params & gen_gettable_params from keygen operation
    
    EVP_PKEY_CTX_gettable_params() was missing code for the keygen operation.
    After adding it it was noticed that it is probably not required for this type, so instead
    the gen_get_params and gen_gettable_params have been remnoved from the provider interface.
    gen_get_params was only implemented for ec to get the curve name. This seems redundant
    since normally you would set parameters into the keygen_init() and then generate a key.
    Normally you would expect to extract data from the key - not the object that we just set up
    to do the keygen.
    
    Added a simple settable and gettable test into a test that does keygen.
    
    Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
    (Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/11683)
